Maslow's hierarchy of needs. A psychological model proposing that human motivation is organized into a pyramid of five levels, from physiological needs at the base through esteem needs to self-actualization at the apex. Abraham Maslow developed the framework in nineteen forty-three, suggesting that individuals must satisfy lower-level needs before pursuing higher ones, though the model's actual predictions have proven more complex than the popular pyramid suggests.

The five levels, from bottom to top, are physiological needs—food, water, sleep. Then safety needs—security and stability. Then love and belonging—relationships and community. Then esteem needs—respect, confidence, achievement. And finally self-actualization at the peak—fulfilling one's potential.

Maslow presented the hierarchy as a theory of human motivation, arguing that unsatisfied needs drive behavior and that satisfaction of lower needs creates space for higher pursuits. The pyramid has become ubiquitous in business, management, and psychology curricula, making it one of the most recognizable models in the social sciences.

But Maslow's original formulation was more flexible than the rigid pyramid suggests. He acknowledged that people sometimes pursue higher needs despite unmet lower ones. Artists starve for their craft, for example. The hierarchy is also culturally situated. Research suggests different cultures prioritize needs in different orders. Western individualism emphasizes self-actualization while other cultures prioritize group belonging earlier. Empirical testing of the hierarchy has not strongly supported the strict five-level model or the idea that lower needs must be fully satisfied before higher ones emerge.

Despite these limitations, the concept influenced humanistic psychology, organizational theory, and modern positive psychology, which extended his focus on human flourishing. Maslow later added a sixth level above self-actualization: self-transcendence, or the pursuit of meaning beyond oneself through spirituality, creativity, or service to others.

Critiques note that the model overlooks that deprivation like poverty and trauma doesn't necessarily prevent higher-level pursuits, and that needs are not always arranged hierarchically but operate simultaneously. Yet the hierarchy resonates because it offers an intuitive framework for understanding why people act as they do, even though it oversimplifies the complex, non-linear nature of actual human motivation.
